title: Binary Search & Greedy
scopeHtml: Scope: classic binary search, boundary search, binary search on the answer, greedy with proof, rotated arrays.

notes.title: Binary search on a sorted array
notes.html:
Idea. If the data is sorted (or monotonic), look at the middle and discard half. Halving each step gives O(log n): a billion elements need only about 30 comparisons.

Recognise it when: sorted input, "find first/last position", "insert position", or any yes/no question that flips exactly once as an index grows.

The safe template keeps an invariant: the answer, if it exists, is always inside [lo, hi].

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int binarySearch(const vector<int>& a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = (int)a.size() - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;            // avoids int overflow of lo + hi
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
int binarySearch(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;            // avoids int overflow of lo + hi
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
fun binarySearch(a: IntArray, target: Int): Int {
    var lo = 0
    var hi = a.size - 1
    while (lo <= hi) {
        val mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2             // avoids int overflow of lo + hi
        when {
            a[mid] == target -> return mid
            a[mid] < target -> lo = mid + 1
            else -> hi = mid - 1
        }
    }
    return -1
}
def binary_search(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2                     # Python ints do not overflow
        if a[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if a[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1

Library versions. C++ lower_bound / upper_bound; Java Arrays.binarySearch / Collections.binarySearch; Kotlin binarySearch(); Python bisect.bisect_left / bisect_right. Know them, but be able to write the loop.

Complexity. O(log n) time, O(1) space.

Industry examples. git bisect finds the commit that introduced a bug by binary searching history; databases binary search inside B-tree pages; autocomplete searches a sorted dictionary.

Everyday analogy. Guessing a number from 1 to 100: ask "higher or lower?" and halve the range each time.

Common interview traps.

  • mid = (lo + hi) / 2 overflows in C++/Java when lo + hi > 2^31 - 1.
  • Infinite loops from lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 with the wrong loop condition.
  • Using it on unsorted data.

notes.title: First and last position (boundary search)
notes.html:
Idea. For duplicates, search for a boundary instead of an exact match: the first index where a[i] >= target (lower bound). The last occurrence is lowerBound(target + 1) - 1.

Template for "first index where condition is true". Use a half-open range [lo, hi); shrink to the boundary:

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int lowerBound(const vector<int>& a, int target) {      // first i with a[i] >= target
    int lo = 0, hi = a.size();                          // hi is exclusive
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] >= target) hi = mid;                 // mid might be the answer
        else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}

vector<int> searchRange(vector<int>& a, int target) {
    int first = lowerBound(a, target);
    if (first == (int)a.size() || a[first] != target) return {-1, -1};
    return {first, lowerBound(a, target + 1) - 1};
}
int lowerBound(int[] a, int target) {                   // first i with a[i] >= target
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length;                          // hi is exclusive
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] >= target) hi = mid;                 // mid might be the answer
        else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}

int[] searchRange(int[] a, int target) {
    int first = lowerBound(a, target);
    if (first == a.length || a[first] != target) return new int[]{-1, -1};
    return new int[]{first, lowerBound(a, target + 1) - 1};
}
fun lowerBound(a: IntArray, target: Int): Int {         // first i with a[i] >= target
    var lo = 0
    var hi = a.size                                     // hi is exclusive
    while (lo < hi) {
        val mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
        if (a[mid] >= target) hi = mid else lo = mid + 1
    }
    return lo
}

fun searchRange(a: IntArray, target: Int): IntArray {
    val first = lowerBound(a, target)
    if (first == a.size || a[first] != target) return intArrayOf(-1, -1)
    return intArrayOf(first, lowerBound(a, target + 1) - 1)
}
from bisect import bisect_left

def search_range(a, target):
    first = bisect_left(a, target)                      # first i with a[i] >= target
    if first == len(a) or a[first] != target:
        return [-1, -1]
    return [first, bisect_left(a, target + 1) - 1]

Complexity. O(log n) for each boundary.

Why half-open works. With [lo, hi), hi = mid keeps mid as a candidate and lo = mid + 1 discards it, so the range always shrinks and the loop ends with lo == hi at the boundary.

Everyday analogy. Finding the first page of a chapter in a thick book: you flip to the middle and ask "have I reached the chapter yet?".

Common interview traps.

  • Returning any match instead of the first/last when duplicates exist.
  • Forgetting to check first == n before reading a[first].
  • Overflow when target + 1 exceeds the type's maximum.

notes.title: Binary search on the answer
notes.html:
Idea. Sometimes the array is not sorted, but the answer space is monotonic: if a value x works, so does every larger (or smaller) value. Then binary search over possible answers, using a feasibility check that costs O(n).

Recognise it when: "minimise the maximum", "maximise the minimum", "smallest capacity/speed/days such that…", and the check is easy but the optimum is hard.

Worked example: Koko Eating Bananas. Piles p[i], you must finish within h hours; eating at speed k takes ceil(p/k) hours per pile. Find the minimum k. Speed k is feasible if total hours ≤ h, and feasibility is monotonic in k.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int minEatingSpeed(vector<int>& piles, int h) {
    int lo = 1, hi = *max_element(piles.begin(), piles.end());
    while (lo < hi) {
        int k = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        long long hours = 0;
        for (int p : piles) hours += (p + k - 1) / k;          // ceil(p / k)
        if (hours <= h) hi = k;                                // feasible: try slower
        else lo = k + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}
int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
    int lo = 1, hi = Arrays.stream(piles).max().getAsInt();
    while (lo < hi) {
        int k = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        long hours = 0;
        for (int p : piles) hours += (p + k - 1) / k;          // ceil(p / k)
        if (hours <= h) hi = k;                                // feasible: try slower
        else lo = k + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}
fun minEatingSpeed(piles: IntArray, h: Int): Int {
    var lo = 1
    var hi = piles.max()
    while (lo < hi) {
        val k = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
        val hours = piles.sumOf { ((it + k - 1) / k).toLong() }  // ceil(p / k)
        if (hours <= h) hi = k else lo = k + 1                   // feasible: try slower
    }
    return lo
}
def min_eating_speed(piles, h):
    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)
    while lo < hi:
        k = (lo + hi) // 2
        hours = sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles)             # ceil(p / k)
        if hours <= h:
            hi = k                                                # feasible: try slower
        else:
            lo = k + 1
    return lo

Complexity. O(n log M) where M is the largest pile: log M iterations, each an O(n) check.

Industry examples. Capacity planning ("smallest number of servers that meet the SLA"), shipping and scheduling problems, and tuning thresholds against a monotonic quality metric.

Everyday analogy. Finding the lowest oven temperature that still bakes the cake in time: test a temperature, adjust up or down.

Common interview traps.

  • Not proving the feasibility predicate is monotonic.
  • Wrong search bounds (lower bound too high or upper bound too low).
  • Integer division rounding: use ceiling division and long for totals.

notes.title: Greedy choices and exchange arguments
notes.html:
Idea. A greedy algorithm makes the best-looking choice at each step and never reconsiders. It is correct only when a local choice can be shown to be part of some optimal solution (the exchange argument: swap any optimal solution's first choice for the greedy one without making it worse).

Recognise it when: scheduling, covering, "minimum number of ..." where sorting by one key reveals the choice.

Worked example: Jump Game (can you reach the last index if a[i] is the maximum jump length from i?). Track the farthest index reachable; if you reach an index beyond it, fail.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool canJump(vector<int>& a) {
    int far = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        if (i > far) return false;               // gap: cannot reach i
        far = max(far, i + a[i]);
    }
    return true;
}
boolean canJump(int[] a) {
    int far = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (i > far) return false;               // gap: cannot reach i
        far = Math.max(far, i + a[i]);
    }
    return true;
}
fun canJump(a: IntArray): Boolean {
    var far = 0
    for (i in a.indices) {
        if (i > far) return false                // gap: cannot reach i
        far = maxOf(far, i + a[i])
    }
    return true
}
def can_jump(a):
    far = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        if i > far:
            return False                         # gap: cannot reach i
        far = max(far, i + x)
    return True

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space.

Classic greedy problems. Activity selection (sort by end time), merge/insert intervals, assign cookies, gas station, Huffman coding, minimum platforms. When greedy is not correct (coin change with arbitrary coins, 0/1 knapsack), use dynamic programming.

Everyday analogy. Packing a bag: always taking the heaviest item first can fail; sometimes a different order is needed, which is why you must justify greedy.

Common interview traps.

  • Using greedy without a proof; always test a counter-example (coin change with coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6).
  • Sorting by the wrong key (end time, not start time, for activity selection).

notes.title: Rotated sorted array
notes.html:
Idea. A sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot ([4,5,6,7,0,1,2]) still has structure: at least one half of any [lo, hi] range is sorted. Decide which half is sorted, check whether the target lies in it, and discard the other half.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int searchRotated(vector<int>& a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = (int)a.size() - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[lo] <= a[mid]) {                                   // left half sorted
            if (a[lo] <= target && target < a[mid]) hi = mid - 1;
            else lo = mid + 1;
        } else {                                                 // right half sorted
            if (a[mid] < target && target <= a[hi]) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
int searchRotated(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[lo] <= a[mid]) {                                   // left half sorted
            if (a[lo] <= target && target < a[mid]) hi = mid - 1;
            else lo = mid + 1;
        } else {                                                 // right half sorted
            if (a[mid] < target && target <= a[hi]) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
fun searchRotated(a: IntArray, target: Int): Int {
    var lo = 0
    var hi = a.size - 1
    while (lo <= hi) {
        val mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid
        if (a[lo] <= a[mid]) {                                   // left half sorted
            if (target >= a[lo] && target < a[mid]) hi = mid - 1 else lo = mid + 1
        } else {                                                 // right half sorted
            if (target > a[mid] && target <= a[hi]) lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid - 1
        }
    }
    return -1
}
def search_rotated(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if a[lo] <= a[mid]:                                      # left half sorted
            if a[lo] <= target < a[mid]:
                hi = mid - 1
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        else:                                                    # right half sorted
            if a[mid] < target <= a[hi]:
                lo = mid + 1
            else:
                hi = mid - 1
    return -1

Complexity. O(log n) for distinct values; with duplicates worst case degrades to O(n) because a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi] hides which half is sorted.

Everyday analogy. A circular clock dial that starts at an arbitrary hour: one side of any slice is still in order.

Common interview traps.

  • < instead of <= in a[lo] <= a[mid] when the range has two elements.
  • Assuming distinct values; duplicates need a lo++/hi-- shrink step.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Binary search halves a sorted or monotonic space; use lo + (hi - lo) / 2, keep a clear invariant, and prefer the half-open lower-bound template for first/last positions. When the array is not sorted but feasibility is monotonic, binary search the answer with an O(n) check. Greedy works when an exchange argument proves the local choice safe (jump game, interval scheduling); otherwise use DP. For a rotated sorted array, one half is always sorted: test whether the target lies in it. Watch overflow, duplicates and off-by-one errors.

questions.promptHtml: Write binary search and explain two bugs that commonly appear in it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Famously easy to get subtly wrong; it reveals discipline with invariants.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep lo and hi as the inclusive range that could still contain the target, compute mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, and move lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid - 1. The two classic bugs are integer overflow in (lo + hi) / 2 and infinite loops from not excluding mid when moving a bound.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The invariant is "if the target exists, it is in [lo, hi]". Each step either returns or removes mid from the range, so the range strictly shrinks and the loop terminates in O(log n).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int binarySearch(const vector<int>& a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = (int)a.size() - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
int binarySearch(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
fun binarySearch(a: IntArray, target: Int): Int {
    var lo = 0
    var hi = a.size - 1
    while (lo <= hi) {
        val mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
        when {
            a[mid] == target -> return mid
            a[mid] < target -> lo = mid + 1
            else -> hi = mid - 1
        }
    }
    return -1
}
def binary_search(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if a[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• (lo + hi) / 2 overflows in C++ and Java for large indices.
  • Writing lo = mid with while (lo < hi) and a floor midpoint, causing an infinite loop.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if there are duplicates and you need the first? → Boundary (lower bound) search.
  2. Complexity? → O(log n) time, O(1) space.
  3. Does a recursive version differ? → Same logic, O(log n) stack.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states the invariant and chooses the template for the problem type.

questions.promptHtml: Find the first and last positions of a target in a sorted array with duplicates in O(log n).

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests boundary searches and half-open ranges.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Write a lowerBound that returns the first index with value ≥ target using a half-open range [lo, hi). The first occurrence is lowerBound(target) if the value matches, and the last is lowerBound(target + 1) - 1. Two O(log n) searches.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
In [lo, hi), hi = mid keeps mid as a candidate while lo = mid + 1 discards it, so the loop ends with lo == hi at the boundary. Always check first < n and a[first] == target before trusting the result.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int lowerBound(const vector<int>& a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.size();
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] >= target) hi = mid;
        else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}
vector<int> searchRange(vector<int>& a, int t) {
    int f = lowerBound(a, t);
    if (f == (int)a.size() || a[f] != t) return {-1, -1};
    return {f, lowerBound(a, t + 1) - 1};
}
int lowerBound(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] >= target) hi = mid;
        else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}
int[] searchRange(int[] a, int t) {
    int f = lowerBound(a, t);
    if (f == a.length || a[f] != t) return new int[]{-1, -1};
    return new int[]{f, lowerBound(a, t + 1) - 1};
}
fun lowerBound(a: IntArray, target: Int): Int {
    var lo = 0
    var hi = a.size
    while (lo < hi) {
        val mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
        if (a[mid] >= target) hi = mid else lo = mid + 1
    }
    return lo
}
fun searchRange(a: IntArray, t: Int): IntArray {
    val f = lowerBound(a, t)
    if (f == a.size || a[f] != t) return intArrayOf(-1, -1)
    return intArrayOf(f, lowerBound(a, t + 1) - 1)
}
from bisect import bisect_left

def search_range(a, t):
    f = bisect_left(a, t)
    if f == len(a) or a[f] != t:
        return [-1, -1]
    return [f, bisect_left(a, t + 1) - 1]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning any match, not the first or last.
  • Indexing a[f] when f == n.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Count occurrences? → last - first + 1.
  2. Insert position? → lowerBound(target).
  3. Floating-point values? → Binary search for a fixed number of iterations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows the library functions but also writes the loop with a clear invariant.

questions.promptHtml: What does "binary search on the answer" mean? Solve Koko Eating Bananas with it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A pattern recognition test for optimisation problems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When the input is not sorted but feasibility is monotonic in the answer (if speed k works, any faster speed works), you can binary search over answer values and use an O(n) check for each. For Koko, the minimum speed k such that the total hours ≤ h is found in O(n log max(pile)).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Define feasible(k); it is false for small k and true for large k. Search the smallest true value: if feasible, hi = k, else lo = k + 1. Use ceiling division and 64-bit totals.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python

    int lo = 1, hi = *max_element(piles.begin(), piles.end());
    while (lo < hi) {
        int k = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        long long hours = 0;
        for (int p : piles) hours += (p + k - 1) / k;
        if (hours <= h) hi = k; else lo = k + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}
int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
    int lo = 1, hi = Arrays.stream(piles).max().getAsInt();
    while (lo < hi) {
        int k = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        long hours = 0;
        for (int p : piles) hours += (p + k - 1) / k;
        if (hours <= h) hi = k; else lo = k + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}
fun minEatingSpeed(piles: IntArray, h: Int): Int {
    var lo = 1
    var hi = piles.max()
    while (lo < hi) {
        val k = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
        val hours = piles.sumOf { ((it + k - 1) / k).toLong() }
        if (hours <= h) hi = k else lo = k + 1
    }
    return lo
}
def min_eating_speed(piles, h):
    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)
    while lo < hi:
        k = (lo + hi) // 2
        if sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles) <= h:
            hi = k
        else:
            lo = k + 1
    return lo

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not checking that feasibility is monotonic.
  • Wrong bounds or floor instead of ceiling division.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Split array largest sum? → Same pattern: search the largest-sum cap, check with a greedy count of pieces.
  2. Capacity to ship packages in D days? → Same pattern.
  3. Square root of x? → Binary search for the largest k with k·k ≤ x.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior identifies the monotonic predicate and justifies the bounds.

questions.promptHtml: How do you know a greedy algorithm is correct? Show an example where greedy fails.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Greedy is often guessed; interviewers want justification.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Prove with an exchange argument: take any optimal solution, show you can swap its first choice for the greedy choice without making it worse, then repeat. Greedy fails for coin change with coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6: greedy takes 4+1+1 (3 coins) but 3+3 uses 2, so DP is needed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Greedy needs the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. Activity selection is correct when sorting by earliest end time because an earlier finishing activity leaves at least as much room as any other first choice. Jump Game works by tracking the farthest reachable index.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool canJump(vector<int>& a) {
    int far = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        if (i > far) return false;
        far = max(far, i + a[i]);
    }
    return true;
}
boolean canJump(int[] a) {
    int far = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (i > far) return false;
        far = Math.max(far, i + a[i]);
    }
    return true;
}
fun canJump(a: IntArray): Boolean {
    var far = 0
    for (i in a.indices) {
        if (i > far) return false
        far = maxOf(far, i + a[i])
    }
    return true
}
def can_jump(a):
    far = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        if i > far:
            return False
        far = max(far, i + x)
    return True

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing greedy because it "feels right" with no counter-example search.
  • Sorting by the wrong key.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Minimum jumps? → Greedy BFS levels, O(n).
  2. Interval scheduling vs weighted? → Unweighted greedy; weighted needs DP.
  3. Fractional vs 0/1 knapsack? → Greedy works for fractional only.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior gives the exchange argument and a counter-example.

questions.promptHtml: Search for a target in a rotated sorted array in O(log n). What changes if there are duplicates?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests reasoning about partial order.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: At each step one half of [lo, hi] is sorted. Compare a[lo] and a[mid] to find which, check whether the target lies inside that sorted half, and discard the other half. With duplicates a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi] makes the sorted half ambiguous, so you shrink by one on each side and the worst case becomes O(n).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The pivot splits the array into two sorted runs, and any window containing the pivot has exactly one sorted side. The <= in a[lo] <= a[mid] handles two-element ranges.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int searchRotated(vector<int>& a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = (int)a.size() - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[lo] <= a[mid]) {
            if (a[lo] <= target && target < a[mid]) hi = mid - 1;
            else lo = mid + 1;
        } else {
            if (a[mid] < target && target <= a[hi]) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
int searchRotated(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[lo] <= a[mid]) {
            if (a[lo] <= target && target < a[mid]) hi = mid - 1;
            else lo = mid + 1;
        } else {
            if (a[mid] < target && target <= a[hi]) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
fun searchRotated(a: IntArray, target: Int): Int {
    var lo = 0
    var hi = a.size - 1
    while (lo <= hi) {
        val mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid
        if (a[lo] <= a[mid]) {
            if (target >= a[lo] && target < a[mid]) hi = mid - 1 else lo = mid + 1
        } else {
            if (target > a[mid] && target <= a[hi]) lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid - 1
        }
    }
    return -1
}
def search_rotated(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if a[lo] <= a[mid]:
            if a[lo] <= target < a[mid]:
                hi = mid - 1
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        else:
            if a[mid] < target <= a[hi]:
                lo = mid + 1
            else:
                hi = mid - 1
    return -1

sections.html:
• Using < instead of <= for the sorted-half test.
  • Assuming O(log n) with duplicates.

1. Find the minimum? → Compare a[mid] with a[hi].
  2. Find the rotation count? → Index of the minimum.
  3. Duplicates variant? → Shrink lo++, hi-- when all three equal.

sections.html: Senior states the O(n) duplicate worst case and why.

questions.contextHtml: A video platform must split 10 million uploaded clips (each with a known processing time, in order) into at most 500 consecutive batches processed in parallel. Batches must preserve order and the total time is set by the slowest batch. Product wants the smallest possible maximum batch time. Your first idea, trying every possible maximum, is too slow.
questions.promptHtml: How do you compute the minimal possible maximum batch time efficiently?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Dynamic programming over partitions with O(n²·k) time, which cannot run for n = 10 million.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must batches be contiguous? Time values integer? Is there a lower bound on batch size?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; algorithm design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: DP is too heavy; the objective is monotonic in the cap, so binary search on the cap.
  4. How I'd verify: For a candidate cap, greedily fill batches: start a new batch when adding the next clip would exceed the cap; count batches.
  5. Root cause: The answer space is monotonic: if cap C works (≤ 500 batches), any larger cap works too.
  6. Fix: Binary search between max(clip time) and sum(all); check feasibility in O(n) with the greedy fill; return the smallest feasible cap. Total O(n log(sum)). With sums up to 10^13 that is about 44 iterations over 10^7 clips.
  7. Prevention: Use 64-bit integers; test with k = 1 (answer = sum) and k = n (answer = max).
  8. Trade-offs: Exact and fast; assumes contiguous batches. Non-contiguous assignment is a bin-packing problem (NP-hard) and would need heuristics.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Streaming data that arrives continuously? → Re-run on windows or use approximate heuristics.
  • Parallelise the check? → Chunked prefix sums, but the greedy scan is sequential.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A job-scheduling service replaced a quadratic partition search with a binary search on the cap and cut planning time from minutes to under a second.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tries every cap.
  • Hire: binary search on the answer with a greedy check.
  • Strong hire: justifies monotonicity, sets bounds, handles 64-bit sums and discusses non-contiguous variants.
